newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Enlargement, EMU to mark Luxembourg EU presidency.
newsitem.headline: Enlargement, EMU to mark Luxembourg EU presidency.

text.p: The European Union's smallest country takes over the EU driving seat on Tuesday with the delicate task of preparing the bloc for eastward expansion and keeping single currency plans on track.
"Our presidency will be dominated by one big subject -- enlargement," Luxembourg's permanent representative to the EU, Jean-Jacques Kasel, said ahead of the Grand Duchy's six-month stint.

Membership talks with central and eastern European countries wanting to join the wealthy western club are due to start six months after the agreement of a new EU treaty, which was reached on June 17 at a summit in Amsterdam.
The presidency must now work out the method by which enlargement talks will proceed, and with how many countries.
But although enlargement is the formal goal of the presidency, troubles over economic and monetary union (EMU) are just as likely to demand reluctant attention as they did the Dutch.
A rift between EU giants France and Germany over how to achieve EMU is likely to dominate the debate for much of the presidency.

But Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker of Luxembourg, whose population is only 413,000, is well placed to handle it as he is also finance minister and has previously taken a mediating role between Paris and Bonn.
EU diplomats, meanwhile, are hopeful the preparations for enlargement can be completed by December.
However, there are concerns that the EU leaders' failure in Amsterdam to agree internal EU reforms could delay the day the aspirants are finally welcomed into the bloc.

Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Lithuania, Latvia, Bulgaria and Romania are all candidates and on July 16 the European Commission is due to publish its recommendations on their readiness to join.

Meanwhile, details of the Amsterdam treaty which were glossed over during the frantic two-day summit must still be hammered out in the weeks ahead under the Luxembourg presidency before a legal text can be written up and signed, probably in October.
On EMU, which it describes as the EU's "last big ambition this century", Luxembourg must ensure nothing threatens the timetable that will see a single European currency introduced on January 1, 1999.
"We will have to keep EMU on track, so that the ignition is ready for Britain to start the engine (next spring)," Kasel said, speaking at the Centre for European Policy Studies in Brussels.
A decision is expected around April or May, under the British EU presidency, on which countries will be in the first wave to take part in the single currency.
Admission will be based on 1997 finances and Luxembourg has already said it wants consideration given to how to limit any speculation in the financial markets in the run-up to that decision.

Amid demands, notably from the French, that the EU be as committed to fighting jobs as it is to EMU, Luxembourg has also agreed to hold a special summit on jobs, though has warned against expecting too much.

"We have a mandate. We must (try and fulfil it)", Kasel said. But he added that the summit must not simply recycle old job-creation ideas. "We must coordinate our policies and generate collective added value," he said.

He echoed comments from Juncker, who reiterated in an interview published in the Belgian newspaper La Libre Belgique that there was "no hope of seeing the Luxembourg presidency present miracle solutions to the problem of unemployment".

Other issues on Luxembourg's six-month agenda will include fiscal harmonisation, the fight against organised crime, more cooperation in acting against drugs as well as a busy schedule on external relations.
Fiscal harmonisation is a particularly sensitive area for Luxembourg because it is renowned for its status as a financial centre and tax haven.
Luxemburg says it does not oppose fiscal streamlining.

But it insists that an agreement should not be limited to tax capital income and should result in a global package which also takes account of taxation on individuals and considers subsidies paid to attract business to a region.
